claims.text: Oxidizing elemental Cr at approximately 900 °C for 10–30 minutes will form a Cr2O3 surface layer.
The pre-formed Cr2O3 layer will be thin, uniform, and adherent.
The pre-formed Cr2O3 layer will be stable and self-limiting under oxidizing conditions.
Cr2O3 passivation will lower oxidation rates in PWR primary water at approximately 320 °C.
The Cr2O3 layer will reduce oxygen ingress into the coating.
A Cr2O3 layer formed on the exposed coating surface will act as a physical barrier to Cr–Zr interdiffusion at the buried Cr–Zr interface.
The pre-formed Cr2O3 layer will remain protective during steam transients approaching 1200 °C.
Pre-oxidized Cr coatings will have significantly lower oxidation rates than as-deposited Cr coatings.
Pre-oxidized Cr coatings will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than as-deposited Cr coatings.
Suppressing oxidation and Cr–Zr interdiffusion will improve coating integrity and long-term durability.
The durability improvement will extend across both PWR primary-water exposure and high-temperature steam exposure.
Unmodified elemental Cr-coated zirconium alloy suffers uncontrolled oxidation in reactor water and high-temperature steam.
Unmodified elemental Cr-coated zirconium alloy suffers excessive Cr–Zr interdiffusion under the stated exposures.
The proposed treatment is applicable after exposures of up to 60 days in approximately 320 °C PWR water and during short steam transients up to 1200 °C.
Thermal cycling may cause long-term mechanical instability or spallation of the pre-formed Cr2O3 scale.

contradictions.description: The intervention explicitly forms Cr2O3 on the exposed outer surface, but the mediator and mechanism treat that surface scale as a physical diffusion barrier at the spatially separate, buried Cr–Zr interface.
The mechanism characterizes Cr2O3 as stable under oxidizing conditions through a boundary reaching 1200 °C, whereas cited evidence states that chromia can form volatile CrO3 above 900 °C.
